text: Few subjects provoke as much disagreement as the question of how we ought to resolve a genuine moral dilemma. Were ethics purely a matter of personal conscience, there would be little need for shared principles at all; nevertheless, most societies expect some baseline of integrity from their citizens, whatever their private beliefs. Consider a classic utilitarian scenario, in which one must weigh up the greatest good for the greatest number against the rights of a single individual. A strictly principled thinker might refuse to compromise on moral obligation under any circumstances, whereas a more pragmatic one would argue that context justifies flexibility. Herein lies the danger many philosophers warn against: the slippery slope by which one seemingly reasonable exception opens the door to further compromise, until what was once condemned as unethical is quietly condoned. Accountability, in this light, becomes essential—not merely punishing wrongdoing after the fact, but ensuring that those with power cannot exploit others and simply get away with it. Nor is hypocrisy easily avoided; even the most impartial observer occasionally fails to live up to standards they demand of others. What remains clear, however, is that questionable shortcuts rarely go without ramifications, however selfless their original intention may have seemed.
